speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It did not seem so long ago that peak hour congestion on our public transport was a common grouse among commuters and it has actually increased now, the peak hour congestion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the course of a year, COVID-19 pandemic has dealt us a vastly different set challenges as a result reduced ridership and changing travel patterns.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whether demand for public transport services will rebound remains to be seen.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Singapore, public transport remains the cleanest way to move large masses of people around.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It builds the foundation of our car-lite vision.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: According to a recent report by the Institute of Policy Studies, our citizens are increasingly taking an interest in environmental issues and prioritising them among their key concerns, even above economy and jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must capitalise on this opportunity and include greener transport in our 2040 Vision.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also need a transport system that is affordable all and sustainable to run.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Barring environmental benefits, the changing patterns of travel poses a conundrum.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has given rise to concerns about the economic viability of our public transport industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think it is timely for all stakeholders, Singaporeans and MOT, to discuss and address this issue over time, especially so now in this new normal environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the years, our public transport network has grown increasingly sophisticated and integrated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Commuters are making more transfers during trips but the trips are shorter.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Now there are many integrated routes to get to your destination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The average fares are lower, especially for bus trips.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In previous fare review exercises, the actual fare increase was found to be less than that determined by the current fare adjustment formula.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has had an adverse impact on the financials of the industry, as the additional fare revenue could never fully compensate for cost increases in operations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite the dip in ridership, service capacity and headways must be preserved to ensure safe distancing measures can be practised.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The introduction of additional disinfection procedures, protection equipment and safe distancing personnel only lead to increased costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Of course, we must also factor in maintenance costs as our rail and bus system ages.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as we embrace these changes, are they financially sustainable on the current operational model?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is worrying is that in most discussions on sustainability now, the emphasis has been on environmental sustainability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The neglect of financial sustainability has been an important omission.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Improving the financial sustainability of public transport would help to realise potential environmental and social benefits of public transport since it would make expanded public transport service more affordable, both for the governments who provide it and for the passengers who use it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Germany and the US offer interesting contrast in the financial sustainability of our public transport.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the past decades, Germany has improved its public transport services, increase productivity, reduce costs, cut subsidy requirements and attracted more passengers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: American public transport systems have improved and expanded services but at a far higher cost, requiring much larger government subsidies and attracting fewer additional riders.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Singapore's case, are we at risk of skewing towards the American trajectory?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to strike a balance between ensuring financial sustainability for operators while keeping fares affordable in this difficult climate and maintaining the quality of service and ease of access to areas which are far from transport nodes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we also explore ways to maximise even more non-fare revenues from ads and retail business, property rentals and other value capture mechanism such as click and collect at transit stations?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we also explore other financing options such as private investments?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we need also to focus on encouraging higher usage of public transport.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, can we encourage transport operators to explore a new integrated mobility ticket or enhance our existing offerings by providing free access to all transit services, including reduced rates for taxis, car-sharing services and rental cars as well as discounts for other services, such as bicycle maintenance and travel information services?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, can we also explore linking e-tickets for large events such as professional soccer games and music concerts, generally also serving as transit tickets to access and leave the venue at no extra charge?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, we should ensure existing feeder bus routes are efficiently linked to different MRT rail nodes, especially the new ones.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fourth, to ensure fares are affordable for financially needy commuters, I would like to suggest we ensure fare concessions extended to also assist adult learner students who may have stopped work or are increasingly going back to night or part-time school to upgrade their skills.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chairman, I would like to declare my interest for being part of the ComfortDelGro management team for the rest of my MOT cuts.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Singapore’s public transport system has been ranked the best in the world in 2020 by consulting firm, Oliver Wyman and the University of California, Berkeley.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In 2018, McKinsey ranked the Singapore public transport system the second best in the world after Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But our transport fare is the most affordable in the world, according to McKinsey.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many thanks to the public transport workers, MOT and LTA for making this possible.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: What is the cost of achieving the most affordable public transport in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In evaluating public transport affordability, McKinsey considered the monthly cost of public transport relative to residents' income, that is, the methodology is not looking at the absolute cost of the public transport fare alone but in relation to the income level of each city.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Using this objective model, McKinsey concluded that the public transport in Singapore is the most affordable in the world.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, public transport fare is a sensitive topic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Very few people in Singapore would openly agree that the public transport fare in Singapore is affordable.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Most people would want public transport fare to be free.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For bus operations, the capital cost is relatively low as compared to the train system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Earlier in the Budget debate, I spoke on the need to revamp the bus routes to be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For train operations, the most profitable train operator in the world is Hong Kong MTR which uses the rail plus property model.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Hong Kong government is the majority shareholder of MTR and it gives land and development rights to MTR at the greenfield price, that is, the price of the land before the railway is built.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: MTR subsequently builds malls, offices and private residential houses around the MRT stations and collects lucrBative rent to subsidise the train operation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In Singapore, revenue from land sales are channelled into the Government's reserve.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: No other major train operator in the world is making money.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: SMRT and Downtown Line Pte Ltd have been losing money for the past few years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But why was SMRT so profitable in the earlier years?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In 2015, the mean kilometres between failures or MKBF for the Singapore rail network was 133,000 train-km.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The dramatic improvements were due to the hard work of public transport workers, MOT and LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, such improvements would not be easy to achieve if not because of the new rail financing framework or NRFF that came into effect since 2016.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Without going into technical details, the NRFF allows the train operators to shift the revenue risk to LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This was especially crucial during the COVID-19 pandemic when the ridership plunged, and so did the fare collection.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The question is whether LTA is prepared to take on the full revenue risk just like the Bus Contracting Model?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is so that the train operators can concentrate in operational excellence at the lowest possible cost without worrying about fare revenue collection and fluctuation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If so, will the Government have to subsidise the train operations even more?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If not, could we maintain our excellent MKBF records?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I know it is a fine balance, but as a responsible Government, we have to make tough choices and not kick the can down the road for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, during the Budget debate, I spoke about the implications of the work-from-anywhere and work-from-home phenomena.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: COVID-19 has transformed our travel patterns, due to the changes in the way we live and the way we work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Has peak-travel public transport commuter load returned to pre-COVID levels, or are we in a new normal situation due to staggered working hours, split-team and telecommuting arrangements?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Should we review our public transport provisions, which were developed in the pre-COVID days, to account for these changes?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, the drop in ridership due to the safe management measures taken to combat the pandemic has worsened the situation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We need to also ensure fair renumeration for the more than 20,000 workers who work tirelessly, day and night, to keep our public transport system operating smoothly and safely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Perhaps, it is time that we review our Bus Contracting Model, which was introduced in 2016.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With our expanding MRT network, is the traditional hub-and-spoke model of our public bus operations still relevant?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Will we consider affordable on-demand bus services to replace trunk and cross-island bus services that incur high costs, but have low commuter load?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To minimise our carbon emissions from land transport, we need to have more people using the public transport system as their preferred or default mode of travel.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MRT and buses are the greenest, cleanest and most efficient people-mover.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry have the latest updates on the usage of our MRT and buses?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of flexi-work and work from home.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Working arrangements and commuting trends has been affected significantly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How does MOT assess the impact of this new circumstance on our public transport usage in the near future and what are the plans to adapt the operations of our MRT and buses to the new norm?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government had announced the expansion plans for our MRT network.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the projections for other financial outlays, such as maintenance and replacement works, which need to be paid by the Government to keep our public transport system going?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As MOT introduced new MRT lines and bus services, fares had been kept affordable.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, this also meant that fare revenues could not keep pace with cost increases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government has been subsidising bus and rail fares and operations heavily.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Government funds are finite and the subsidies cannot keep increasing.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need a system that is both affordable for all to use and is sustainable for us to run.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All of us – commuters, operators, Government – have to play our parts for our public transport system to work, and work well.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we rely on technology to achieve this?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Presently, transport demand is unevenly spread between peak and non-peak periods.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have apps for people to check bus schedules and arrivals.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps some form of pre-booking may be helpful for operators to optimise trips, improve efficiency and cut down wastage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The greater the adoption of such apps' utilisation, the better the match between operators and commuters – a win-win situation and a much more sustainable way to move around.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This provision is to deal with the "just-in-case" situations which can potentially leave thousands of commuters without transport.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The advantages of buses is that they are flexible and their routes can be easily adapted for contingencies and emergencies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's Aviation industry has been one of the hardest hit industry in this pandemic, given the sector's complete dependence on international travel.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With the resurgence of COVID-19 in many regions of the world, as well as the emergence of new and more contagious COVID-19 strains, the outlook for the aviation sector remains bleak with air travel likely to be stymied well into this year and next.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I recognise the efforts made to support this industry in terms of re-establishing air travel and supporting airport-related companies and employees through the various support packages previously announced, and the newly announced plans in Budget 2021.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, I wish to clarify with Minister on a few matters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Companies in this sector include those involving maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO), avionics and aircraft component production and repair.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These businesses are essential segments of our aviation supply chain in Singapore, and face major and sustained downstream impact resulting from airlines deferring aircraft orders and reducing their after-market expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Already, we have seen significant retrenchment exercises among a number of key players in the sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With no signs of an immediate recovery for aviation, more of such retrenchments may be expected as companies seek to cut down on their expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even when the air travel does begin to normalise, given that the aviation supply chain is driven by airline demand, aerospace companies could likely be some of the slowest to recover in this hard-hit sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While they still do have continuing GSS support the sector could use more targeted support if we are to maintain our position as an aviation and aerospace hub.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Could the Ministry considered tailored support schemes that could be explored specifically for this group?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Would the Ministry also be able to provide further details of its previously announced plans to develop programmes for aviation workers; at risk of losing their jobs or being unemployed, first mentioned in December last year?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What is the coverage and scale these programmes, and when will they come into effect?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can there be consideration of extending the eligible period of support beyond the current three months, given that the aviation sector is likely to remain impacted by the pandemic for a prolonged period of time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And employees in this niche industry may need more time to secure jobs outside this view, given the need for retraining and reskilling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Lastly, I think there is a need for us to evaluate the upcoming pipeline of talent from our Institutes of Higher Learning into both the aviation and aerospace industries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Fresh graduates from these programmes may find little opportunities there if the global recovery is gradual.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the Minister can assuage these concerns.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman Sir, I declare my interest as an employee of the aviation sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has literally sent our once vibrant and booming aviation sector into a cliff drop.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With the COVID-19 pandemic still raging in many parts of the world, non-essential overseas travel will likely still be curtailed for at least another year, until vaccination operations for the majority of our local population are completed.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Unlike other airports and airlines that are still able to continue to operate domestic flights during this pandemic, Changi Airport and Singapore Airlines group are 100% dependent on international travel.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To the credit of many stakeholders in the aviation sector, tremendous efforts have been made to keep the planes flying, serve passengers and carry cargo, during this extremely difficult period.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: SIA has reconfigured some passenger aircraft for cargo flights and kept key city links connected even with very low passenger loads.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, Sir, I have a few queries relating to our strategies to reboot air travel and to revive the Changi airhub.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Two, beyond the extended JSS and support for the aviation sector as announced in Budget 2021, does the Government intend to continue to support the recovery of the aviation sector and, if so, what are some of these additional support measures for companies and workers?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Three, can the Government provide an update on the developments in the aviation sector since the Ministerial Statement in October 2020?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What has the progress of our measures been so far?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Four, we have seen an increase in the number of imported cases over the past few weeks.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How can we continue to re-open our borders safely?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Five, there have also been a few cases where air crew and other aviation frontline workers who caught COVID-19 earlier this year.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What has the Government done to safeguard our borders and frontline aviation workers?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Six, in a post-vaccination world, what are our plans to open up our borders and revive air travel?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Will vaccinated individuals be allowed to travel with fewer restrictions?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Seven, how can we rebuild the connectivity at Changi Airport and protect our status as an aviation hub?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Lastly, how can we strengthen our competitive advantage to capture air travel demand as it recovers?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope Minister for Transport can inspire hope, confidence and provide guidance through this harsh winter for the aviation industry.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as Advisor to the Singapore Port Workers Union.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We understand that the Maritime sector is the least affected transport segment in the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, the construction sector was badly affected by the circuit breaker last year, which dramatically slowed down the construction schedule of many infrastructural projects.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Was the construction of the Tuas Mega Port affected by COVID-19 pandemic, and by how much?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If so, given the rise of international trade due to the popularity of cross-border online purchases and recovery of the world’s economy from the pandemic over the next few years, are there plans to accelerate the construction of the Tuas Mega Port?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I am also concerned about the accessibility of the Tuas Mega Port for its workers, because unlike the former sites at Tanjong Pagar and Keppel, the Tuas Mega Port is right at the extreme western end of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For the benefit of those who have to travel to the Tuas Mega Port, which will definitely become an activity hub, could the MRT line be extended to the Tuas Mega Port?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Are there plans to provide priority housing in Jurong West for port workers who opt to work in Tuas?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, the Maritime sector remains a crucial pillar of support for our economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In spite of the pandemic, it has remained resilient, thanks to good pandemic safety management along with its global reputation for excellent connectivity and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As other countries are looking to diversify their supply chains to the Southeast Asia region, we can leverage on the sector to strengthen our position.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: During the Committee of Supply debates last year, the Ministry announced that the sustainability remains a key priority.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Indeed, while shipping is one of the world's cleanest and energy-efficient modes of cargo transportation, it leaves a significant environmental footprint.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The Green Energy and Technology Programme, in particular, aims to encourage Singapore-based maritime companies to develop and conduct pilot trials for green technologies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can we leverage on this to create more jobs for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can the Minister share the plans to promote more sustainable practices in the maritime sector?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How will this lead to new and exciting career pathways for locals?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We should not waste this crisis and ensure that we create new jobs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The expedited tax disbursements are certainly well received.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our point-to-point drivers have also raised longer term livelihood concerns due to the prolonged crisis, as well as the evolution of technology in the transport sector.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With long queues at taxi stands, not of passengers, but of taxis themselves, our drivers know that the recovery of the domestic consumer economy will not be the end of their problems.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Instead, our drivers anticipate the re-opening of borders and our night life to give their livelihoods a much-needed boost.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are strange times, as our taxi and PHV drivers trawl our empty streets, night after night, hour after hour, looking for possible passenger.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to practise empathy and, indeed, sympathy towards the plight of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our brothers and sisters are hit with the double whammy of low street hails, having to drive aimlessly around, wasting fuel and time, on having to deal with the petrol tax hikes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will greatly ease the burden and stress of our drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As our drivers focus on getting passengers safely and efficiently to their destinations, we must allay their concerns of obsolescence.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Be it electric or driverless vehicles that hallmark our future, transitions will always require adjustments.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Having undergone technological change with ride-hailing apps, diversifying into transport services like deliveries, or even just facing the economic realities of COVID-19 crisis, our P2P drivers are a resilient bunch.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the Government must anticipate, ease and enable our drivers to prepare for these changes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must not let the P2P transport sector become a byword for creative destruction, just as rickshaws and trishaws are looked upon today, but beckon and support them along the evolution journey of our P2P transport sector.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As far as it may go in pushing the rest of Singapore into a car-lite society, our driver inescapably live in a car-heavy livelihood.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If they are given the support and opportunity to go electric to avoid petrol costs, many would gladly do so.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, their hands are tied, and so the environmental boons become their economic bane.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we must prepare our P2P drivers for the future, could we do more to gird their livelihoods in the present as well?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, I have earlier declared my interest for being part of ComfortDelGro management team.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Would it be possible for LTA to give some insights into the demographics of those who are driving taxis and private-hire cars or PHCs?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Taxis and private-hire cars are collectively called Point-to-Point or P2P vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: My sense is that driving a P2P vehicle has become very popular amongst the youth, especially due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: It is good that they are finding ways to make a living but I do not think it is wise for so many young Singaporeans to be contented with the P2P career as a driver.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In fact, our founding Prime Minister, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, did not want so many Singaporeans driving taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Thus, the growth of taxis was restricted and only Singaporeans above 30 years old could drive the taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The rationale is not to hog too many young people in the driving profession.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This is also in the context of an explosion of P2P vehicles in Singapore in the last decade.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: When Uber officially launched its service eight years ago in Singapore, there were 27,000 taxis and very few PHCs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In totality, there are 2.5 times P2P vehicles today as compared to eight years ago.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Do we really need so many P2P vehicles and drivers in Singapore?

text: The robust transport eco-system in Singapore comprises not just public transport, but also many private transport providers which "fill in the gaps".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Efficient and convenient public transport is vital to achieving many of our national priorities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It enables workers to travel to further out workplaces and it helps us to reach our climate change goals.

text: I sold my car five years ago and now make most of my trips by bus and MRT.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have not regretted this decision and I highly recommend it to others who can afford not to drive.

text: They brought our favourite foods to our doorsteps when we could not dine out and allowed us to eat in the safety of our own homes.
